vulnerability: Stored index becomes invalid when stakeholders withdraw, causing out-of-bounds revert and DoS
reason: The contract uses an EnumerableSet called `stakeholders` and stores a persistent index `lastCompund`. The `_withdraw` function removes an address from `stakeholders` when its balance becomes zero. However, `lastCompund` is never adjusted when the set shrinks. If a stakeholder withdraws and the set length becomes less than or equal to `lastCompund`, the next call to `runCompund` will execute `stakeholders.at(currentIndex)` with an out-of-bounds index, causing a revert. An attacker can exploit this by calling `runCompund` with a small batch size to advance `lastCompund` to the last valid index, then withdrawing their stake (or coordinating multiple withdrawals) to shrink the set below `lastCompund`. This bricks the autocompound functionality until the manager calls `resetLastCompound()`. The attacker can repeat this, causing persistent denial of service. Additionally, EnumerableSet removal uses swap-and-pop, which can shift indices and cause some accounts to be skipped or processed multiple times, leading to unfair rewards distribution.

vulnerability: Public function allows anyone to force compounding and burn fees, causing permanent loss of user rewards
reason: `compundForAccount` is marked `public` and has no access control. It can be called by anyone for any account. The function calculates `performaceTax` and `compundFee`, subtracts them from `rewards[account]`, and then calls `_compound(account)` to compound only the remaining rewards. The deducted fees are not transferred to the fee address or to the caller; they simply remain in the contract as unaccounted tokens (effectively stuck). An attacker can call this function on any stakeholder’s account at any time, permanently reducing that user’s rewards by the fee amounts. This is a griefing attack that causes direct financial loss to victims. The attacker can repeat this for all users, draining their rewards into the contract without any mechanism to recover them. The function should be internal or restricted to be called only by `runCompund` (which properly distributes the fees) or by the account owner.

vulnerability: Missing upper bound allows manager to set fees >100%, causing underflow DoS or theft of all rewards
reason: `setCompundReward` (and similarly `setPerformanceFee`) allows the MANAGER_ROLE to set the compound reward fee to any `uint256` value without an upper bound check. If the fee is set greater than 10,000 (100%), `compundForAccount` will compute `compundFee` such that `compundFee + performaceTax` exceeds `rewards[account]`, causing an arithmetic underflow and reverting the transaction. This bricks both `compundForAccount` and `runCompund`, effectively freezing all autocompounding. More severely, a malicious or compromised manager can set `compundReward` to 10,000 (100%), then call `runCompund` themselves. For each processed account, the entire reward is subtracted as `compundFee` and transferred to `msg.sender` (the manager), stealing all accrued rewards from stakeholders. The same attack is possible via `setPerformanceFee` if the manager controls `taxConfiguration.hpayFeeAddress`. The missing validation makes the protocol highly vulnerable to privileged rug-pulls or accidental misconfiguration.
